questions.explain: The example job rebuilds indexes over 30% fragmentation and reorganizes between 10-30% — it queries current state from the DMV and only does the work that's actually needed, which is idempotent by construction.
options: It rebuilds every index in the database every night at 2 AM.
It only runs on Sundays, when nobody is using the system.
It queries current fragmentation from the DMV and rebuilds or reorganizes only indexes that actually need it, so re-running it is safe and efficient.
It uses SQL Server Agent instead of Task Scheduler.
questions.q: In the chapter's example 'Nightly Index Maintenance' Agent job, what makes the maintenance adaptive (and idempotent by construction)?

questions.explain: ONLINE = ON requires Enterprise edition. The job would fail on Standard — so parameterize the edition check via SERVERPROPERTY('EngineEdition') and degrade gracefully to offline rebuilds inside the maintenance window.
options: ONLINE = ON is only supported on Standard edition.
The job will fail on Standard edition because ONLINE index rebuilds require Enterprise — you must check SERVERPROPERTY('EngineEdition') and degrade gracefully.
Nothing — ONLINE = ON works on all editions.
The job will succeed but silently perform offline rebuilds.
questions.q: What happens if the adaptive index-maintenance job (which uses REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = ON)) runs on SQL Server Standard Edition?

questions.explain: Jobs owned by personal logins break when that login is disabled or leaves the company. Production jobs must be owned by a dedicated service account, with failure notifications and idempotent logic.
options: Every production job must be owned by a dedicated service account, not a personal login.
Jobs must be owned by sa.
Job ownership only matters for SSIS steps, not T-SQL steps.
Ownership is irrelevant because SQL Server Agent runs as SYSTEM.
questions.q: Why does the chapter call job ownership one of the three disciplines of reliable SQL Server Agent automation?

questions.explain: Permission and context differences between your sysadmin SSMS session and the job's runtime are the classic 'works for me' failure — always test maintenance procedures as the Agent service account.
options: Because the Agent service account has no network access.
Because permission and context differences between your session and the job's runtime cause 'works for me' failures — test as the account that will actually run it.
Because SSMS uses a different T-SQL dialect than Agent.
Because Agent jobs cannot use dynamic SQL.
questions.q: Why should you test a maintenance procedure as the SQL Server Agent service account rather than as sysadmin in SSMS?

questions.explain: For SQL Server environments, Database Mail provides native alerting triggerable directly from T-SQL (msdb.dbo.sp_send_dbmail), and SQL Server Agent has built-in alerts for Agent job events, error-log events, and performance conditions — an underused native feature set.
options: SQL Server Agent can only send alerts via PagerDuty.
Database Mail (sp_send_dbmail) can fire email alerts directly from T-SQL, and Agent provides built-in alerts for job events, error-log events, and performance conditions.
SQL Server has no native alerting; you must use Azure Monitor.
Alerting requires the Enterprise edition.
questions.q: What native SQL Server mechanisms can fire alerts without any external scripting layer?
